```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  results = "hide",
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)

theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

# Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r noaa-cleaning}
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables, representing daily weather measurements from NOAA stations in New York State. Key variables include station ID, observation date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperatures.

Missing data are substantial, particularly for temperature measurements: 43.7% of both `tmax` and `tmin` observations are missing. Missingness is also present in precipitation (5.62%), snowfall (14.7%), and snow depth (22.8%). Station IDs and dates have no missing values.

For data cleaning, I extracted year, month, and day from the date variable, converted temperatures to degrees Celsius and precipitation to millimeters, and retained snowfall and snow depth in millimeters.

```{r snowfall-frequency}
snow_frequency =
  noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

head(snow_frequency, 10)
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm (2,008,508 observations), reflecting the fact that snowfall does not occur on most days. Among nonzero values, 25 mm and 13 mm are particularly common, followed by 51 mm and 76 mm. These values approximately correspond to common measurements in inches (1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches), suggesting that rounding and conversion from inches to millimeters contribute to the observed frequencies. Missing snowfall values are excluded from this interpretation.

```{r january-july-temperature, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
monthly_tmax =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

monthly_tmax |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station and Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12)
  )
```
The two-panel plot shows a clear seasonal difference in average maximum temperature. January temperatures generally cluster around 0°C, whereas July temperatures are mostly between 25°C and 30°C. Temperatures across stations tend to fluctuate together over time, suggesting shared year-to-year weather patterns. There are also a few potential outliers, including an unusually low July average around 1988. These observations may reflect unusual weather conditions or limited station-level data and would require further investigation.

```{r temperature-snowfall-plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "A. Daily Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "B. Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  temperature_plot,
  snowfall_plot,
  ncol = 1
)
```
The temperature plot shows a strong positive relationship between daily minimum and maximum temperatures, with most observations concentrated along an upward-sloping band. A few extreme or inconsistent values are visible and may reflect measurement or recording errors.

The snowfall distributions are broadly similar across years, with prominent peaks around 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm. These peaks are consistent with common snowfall measurements originally recorded in inches and converted to millimeters. There is no clear systematic change in the shape of the annual distributions. However, these plots describe the distribution of individual nonzero snowfall observations rather than annual snowfall totals.

# Problem 2

## Data Import and Cleaning

```{r nhanes-import}
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```

```{r nhanes-cleaning}
nhanes_covar_clean =
  nhanes_covar |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_accel_long =
  nhanes_accel |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute)
  )

nhanes_complete =
  nhanes_covar_clean |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel_long, by = "seqn")
```
The demographic and accelerometer datasets each initially contained 250 participants. After excluding individuals younger than 21 and those with missing demographic information, 228 participants remained, including 118 men and 110 women. The accelerometer data were reshaped into long format and merged with demographic information using participant ID (`seqn`). The resulting dataset contains 328,320 observations, corresponding to 1,440 minute-level activity measurements for each of the 228 participants.

## Demographic Summary

```{r education-sex-table, results='asis'}
education_sex_table =
  nhanes_covar_clean |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

education_sex_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education Level", "Men", "Women"),
    caption = "Number of Participants by Education Level and Sex"
  )
```
```{r age-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
nhanes_covar_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1)
  )
```
Among the 228 eligible participants, 118 were men and 110 were women. The largest education group was more than high school (115 participants), followed by high school equivalent (58) and less than high school (55). Sex distributions were relatively balanced in the lowest and highest education categories, while men outnumbered women in the high school equivalent group.

The age distributions suggest that participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger, with median ages in the early 40s, compared with approximately 60 years among those with less than a high school education. Within the high school equivalent group, women have a higher median age than men. However, age distributions overlap considerably across groups.

## Total Daily Activity

```{r total-daily-activity}
nhanes_daily =
  nhanes_complete |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r total-activity-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
nhanes_daily |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
Total daily activity generally decreases with age across education levels, with particularly noticeable declines among older participants. In the high school equivalent group, women show relatively high activity levels around ages 30–40, followed by a decline. In the more than high school group, women tend to have slightly higher smoothed activity levels than men across much of the age range. However, individual variability is substantial, and the smoothed curves should be interpreted cautiously, particularly where observations are sparse. One unusually low activity value is visible among younger men in the highest education category.

## 24-Hour Activity Patterns

```{r hourly-activity-summary}
nhanes_timecourse =
  nhanes_complete |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )
```

```{r activity-timecourse-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
nhanes_timecourse |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.08,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Education and Sex",
    x = "Time of Day (hours)",
    y = "Mean Activity (MIMS/min)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
The 24-hour activity curves show a clear daily pattern across all education levels. Mean activity is lowest during the early morning hours (approximately 3–5 AM), increases rapidly after 6 AM, remains relatively high throughout the daytime, and declines during the evening.

Participants with more than a high school education generally show higher daytime activity than those in the high school equivalent group. Sex differences also vary by education level: women tend to have higher daytime activity than men in the highest education category, whereas the male and female curves are more similar among participants with less than a high school education.

These patterns suggest differences in daily activity timing and intensity across demographic groups, although the observed associations do not establish causal relationships.

# Problem 3

## Data Import and Cleaning

```{r citibike-import}
citi_jan_2020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")

citi_july_2020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv")

citi_jan_2024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")

citi_july_2024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv")
```

```{r citibike-cleaning}
citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    citi_jan_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
    citi_july_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
    citi_jan_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
    citi_july_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2020, 2024)),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )
```

The Citi Bike dataset contains 99,485 sampled rides from January and July of 2020 and 2024. The four CSV files were combined into a single dataset, retaining all original variables and adding year and month indicators. The resulting dataset has 9 variables, including ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration in minutes, starting and ending stations, membership status, year, and month. Categorical variables were converted to factors with meaningful ordering for subsequent tables and visualizations.

## Ridership by Membership Status

```{r citibike-membership-table, results='asis'}
citibike_membership_table =
  citibike_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Total = Casual + Member
  )

citibike_membership_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual Riders", "Members", "Total Rides"),
    caption = "Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Status"
  )
```
Citi Bike members accounted for the majority of rides in all four months. Ridership was substantially higher in July than in January for both years, and the sampled number of rides increased between 2020 and 2024. July 2024 had the highest ridership, with 47,156 rides compared with 18,861 in January 2024.

Casual ridership showed particularly strong seasonality. The proportion of casual rides increased from approximately 7.9% in January to 26.8% in July 2020, and from 11.2% to 23.1% in 2024. This pattern may reflect greater recreational or tourist use during warmer months. These comparisons describe sampled rides rather than the number of unique riders.

## Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024

```{r citibike-top-stations, results='asis'}
top_stations =
  citibike_df |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "rides", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_stations |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting Station", "Number of Rides"),
    caption = "Top 5 Citi Bike Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```
In July 2024, Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most frequently used starting station in the sample, with 163 rides. The five leading stations had relatively similar ride counts, ranging from 146 to 163.

## Median Ride Duration by Day, Month, and Year

```{r citibike-median-duration}
citibike_median =
  citibike_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
```{r citibike-median-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
citibike_median |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = month,
      group = month
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Citi Bike Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
Median ride duration was consistently longer in July than in January across both years and all days of the week. Weekend rides were generally longer than weekday rides, particularly in July 2020, when median durations increased to approximately 16.5 minutes on Saturday and Sunday.

Median ride durations were also shorter in 2024 than in 2020 for corresponding months and weekdays. These differences may reflect changes in rider behavior, trip purposes, or the availability of electric bikes, although the descriptive data cannot establish the underlying causes.

## Ride Duration Distribution in 2024

```{r citibike-duration-distribution, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = rideable_type,
      y = duration,
      fill = member_casual
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.7,
    outlier.alpha = 0.1
  ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution by Bike Type and Membership in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Membership"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
In 2024, casual riders generally had longer ride durations than members across both months and bike types. Ride durations were also typically longer and more variable in July than in January, particularly among casual riders. Differences between classic and electric bikes were present but generally smaller than differences by membership status.

All groups showed right-skewed ride duration distributions, with numerous long-duration outliers. These patterns suggest that membership status and month are associated with substantial differences in typical ride duration, although the data do not establish causal effects.
